# Operational Lifecycle and Production Hardening

The controls in this part decay. ROAs drift away from announcements, certificates expire, and a filter that was right in March accepts a leak in October. This chapter is the operating rhythm that keeps chapter 7 and chapter 12 true: who rotates keys, who tests a change, how much router you need, and what you do when a site fails.

## Learning goals

- Run a ROA and a prefix as one lifecycle, not two tickets
- Rotate RPKI keys and router authentication without a surprise Invalid
- Test policy on fixtures and on a single router before the whole edge
- Size control-plane capacity, and write the failure mode you will accept when a site is lost
- Audit the system against the checklist in chapter 16

## ROA Lifecycle Management at Scale

Every prefix you originate has a row in git. The row names the prefix, the origin AS, the announced length, the ROA `maxLength`, the ticket that justified a wider length if there is one, and the date you last confirmed a looking glass saw it as Valid.

The lifecycle:

| Event | Order of operations |
|-------|---------------------|
| New announcement | Open the row, publish the ROA, wait until your validator has the VRP, then announce |
| More-specific for maintenance | Publish the covering ROA or the extra ROA first. Remove the more-specific and tighten the ROA when the maintenance ends |
| Origin change (new AS, scrubber, acquisition) | Add the new origin to a ROA and confirm Valid before that AS announces. Remove the old origin only after the old AS has stopped announcing |
| Prefix returned to the RIR | Withdraw the announcement, remove the ROA, confirm collectors no longer see it |
| Space you hold and do not announce | Publish an AS0 ROA so a hijack is Invalid rather than NotFound |

Hosted RPKI makes the portal click the easy part and the order the hard part. Delegated RPKI makes the order enforceable in the pipeline from chapter 17, and makes you responsible for publication. Either way, a weekly job diffs the originated list against the VRPs your own validator holds and pages on mismatches. That job is the lifecycle. A ROA you created once at turn-up is not.

Multi-origin during a migration is legitimate. Record the end date on the second origin. The weekly diff should complain about origins that are still authorised and no longer used.

## Key and Certificate Rotation for RPKI

Rotation is planned work.

**Hosted.** The RIR holds the CA keys. Your job is the portal account: who can publish, how that access is revoked when someone leaves, and how you get in when the person who set up single sign-on has left. Exercise the backup access. A ROA you cannot withdraw is a stuck Invalid waiting for a mistake.

**Delegated.** You run the CA. Rotate end-entity keys as the software does by default for each object. Rotate the CA key on a schedule you have rehearsed, with the parent (the RIR) issuing the new certificate before the old one expires. Publication of the new certificate, the new manifests, and the re-signed objects has to overlap the old objects. A gap is a global NotFound or Invalid for your space. Do the first rotation in a lab CA. Do the second on a small real allocation before you do it on the aggregate.

Router-to-cache authentication is a separate rotation. When you change an RTR password, an IPsec key, or a management ACL, one cache at a time, and confirm the router still has the other cache before you touch the second. TCP-AO or MD5 keys on BGP sessions roll with the neighbour's cooperation, one session at a time, with the hold timer as the failure detector if you get it wrong. Have the previous key until the new session is Established.

TAL changes are rare and external. Subscribe to the RIR's trust-anchor announcements. A validator that does not have the new TAL will drop that RIR's VRPs. The alert is the per-RIR VRP count from chapter 18.

## Change Management for BGP Security Policies

Chapter 17 is the pipeline. The lifecycle around it:

- Standard changes (a customer prefix inside their allocation, a quota bump under the agreed ceiling) follow the generator and a peer review
- Exception changes (accept NotFound for one customer, a temporary SLURM, a blackhole) carry an owner and an expiry, and the expiry job is allowed to revert them
- Emergency changes still land in git, the same day, by the incident lead in chapter 19
- Two-person review is the default for export policy and for anything that lowers a max-prefix or widens an allow-list onto a transit session
- Freeze windows exist for the edge during other large network maintenances. A ROA publish during a transit migration makes the timeline unreadable

The question a reviewer answers is the checklist in chapter 16, not "does this syntax compile." A compiled permit-any is a successful build of a bad policy.

## Testing and Validation Procedures

Test at three depths.

**Fixture tests**, on every commit, from chapter 17. Ten routes with known accept or reject results, including an RPKI Invalid and a customer leak. No router required.

**Lab tests**, when the template or the OS version changes. The existing labs in this book (policy, ROV, maxLength, communities, dual-home) are the regression suite for FRR. Re-run the ROV drills after an FRR upgrade before you upgrade the edge. Add a case when chapter 19 discovers a class the fixtures missed.

**Production canaries.** Install the new policy on one router. Compare received and advertised counts, the Invalid drop counter, and a sample of your own prefixes as seen from a collector. Give it a defined soak time before the rest of the edge. A canary that resets its transit session is a failed test, not a reason to push faster to "make them match."

Validation after every ROA publish is a looking-glass or a validator query that shows the intended state. The change is not done when the portal says submitted. It is done when a relying party you do not share a fate with has the VRP.

## Capacity Planning for Routing Infrastructure

Size the control plane for the table you actually take, plus headroom, plus a bad day.

| Speaker | Plan for |
|---------|----------|
| Edge taking a full table | One global IPv4 table and one IPv6 table per transit, twice if you keep a received copy and a selected copy, plus BMP overhead |
| Route reflector | The client count times the best-path table it reflects. Clients do not cost a full table each if you reflect best paths only, and they do cost a session and an update group |
| Validator | CPU and disk for RRDP snapshots of all five RIRs, and a memory footprint that stays flat. A validator that grows without bound is a leak in the validator |
| Collector | BMP update retention for the incident window |

Max-prefix headroom on transit is a capacity choice. Set the reset above normal growth and below the memory you measured. Write down the measurement. A number copied from a conference slide is not a measurement of your route processor.

Feature cost belongs in the same plan. ROV comparison is cheap. Turning on BGPsec-style per-update signatures is not, which is one more reason chapter 10 stays a goal. ASPA path walks, if you enable them, get a lab measurement on a full table before you enable them on the edge.

## Disasters, Failures, and Recovery Plans

Write the routing failure modes the way you write facility failure modes.

| Failure | What must still be true |
|---------|-------------------------|
| One transit session down | The other transit carries your cone. Traffic engineering may be wrong. Reachability is not |
| One validator down | Routers still have the second cache. Alerts fire. Policy does not flip to accept-Invalid |
| Both validators down | Routers keep the last VRPs until expire, then fail open to NotFound. You know the expire value because you set it. You do not drop NotFound |
| One site down | Route reflectors in the other site still see the edge. You did not place every reflector in one failure domain |
| Delegated CA or portal account unavailable | A second operator can publish and can revoke. You tested it |
| Bad policy deployed | The previous git revision can be pushed by someone who is not the person who wrote the bad one |
| You are leaking | Max-prefix or the emergency reject stops export. The communications step in chapter 19 is rehearsed |

Recovery drills are calendar items. Once a year, withdraw a lab prefix and publish a matching ROA in the lab. Once a year, fail a validator and confirm the alert and the remaining cache. Once a year, roll a BGP session password with a willing peer or in the lab. A plan that has not been run is a document.

Backups of the CA state, for delegated RPKI, are security-sensitive material. Store them with the same care as other key material, and test a restore into a lab. A backup you cannot restore is not a backup. Hosted-RPKI operators still export a copy of what they think they published, so a portal outage does not take the inventory with it.

## Auditing, Compliance, and Security Reviews

Audit against the architecture, not against a product logo.

A quarterly review can be a short list:

- Every external neighbour maps to a class template. Orphans are listed
- Every originated prefix has a ROA row and a monitoring row, and the weekly diff is clean
- `maxLength` waivers are in date or gone
- SLURM and blackhole exceptions are empty or in date
- Two validators ran different implementations all quarter, and their VRP counts stayed within the threshold
- Max-prefix warnings were either acted on or had the threshold fixed. There is no warning that has been "known" for months
- The incident tickets from the quarter produced a fixture test or an explicit "we accept this risk"
- Who can publish ROAs, who can deploy policy, and who can log into edge routers is the current staff list

External programmes such as MANRS line up with this list (filtering, anti-spoofing, coordination, global validation information). Use them as a cross-check. Passing a logo and failing the quarterly diff is not the posture this part describes.

Customer and regulator reports should be generated from the same data: the prefix list, the ROA state, the last incident timeline. A report written from memory will disagree with the routers.

## Summary

- A prefix, its ROA, and its alert are one row with an order of operations
- Rotate portal access and delegated CA keys with overlap, one cache or one session at a time
- Review policy as a checklist. Test with fixtures, labs, and a canary router
- Size full tables, reflectors, and validators from measurements, and set max-prefix inside that budget
- Drills for a dead validator, a bad deploy, and a leak are on the calendar
- Quarterly audits read git and the routers. They do not read a slide
